books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales, including The Last of the Mohicans (1826), follow the frontiersman Natty Bumppo through the forests of New York during the wars of the 1700s. Cooper's novels mixed adventure with descriptions of the wilderness, and they sold widely in the United States and in Europe.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 B: Cooper was perhaps the most successful American romantic writer, and his Leatherstocking Tales, including The Last of the Mohicans (1826), captured the danger and fascination of the frontier experience. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Cooper's novels were distinctively American mainly because they did which of the following?

options.text: Retold British legends about kings and castles
options.misconception: Cooper admired the British writer Sir Walter Scott, so it is easy to think he copied Scott's settings.

options.text: Were written in French for European readers
options.misconception: The novels sold in Europe, so it is easy to think they were written for Europeans.

options.text: Copied the style of Sir Walter Scott without any change
options.misconception: Scott's influence was real, so it is easy to turn influence into exact copying.

options.text: Set popular fiction on the American frontier and in its forests

rationales.A: Cooper set his novels in American forests, not in British castles or courts.
rationales.B: Cooper wrote in English; Europeans read him in translation.
rationales.C: Cooper borrowed Scott's romantic spirit but gave it American settings, which is the point of the stimulus.
rationales.D: The frontier, Natty Bumppo, and the wilderness were new subjects, and readers on both sides of the Atlantic loved them.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what is new in the stimulus. A frontiersman in New York forests, not a knight in a castle.
2. Ask why that counts as American. The setting itself — the frontier — had never carried a popular novel before.
Background: Barron's calls Cooper the most successful American romantic writer, rooted in the frontier.
Remember: a new setting can make a whole literature new.
